terms.title: Audit Planning Audit Universe Coverage Ratio
terms.definition: This term measures the proportion of the relevant audit population, requirement or work area that has been included in the audit scope, work programme or executed testing. for the complete set of auditable entities, processes, systems, locations, risk themes and assurance objects from which the audit plan is built. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Audit Universe Items Covered / Total Audit Universe Items
terms.components: Covered: included in audit/testing; Total: audit population. Confirm that the denominator is the complete approved population and that exclusions are documented.
terms.howToUse: Use it to challenge whether the audit work covers the intended population and whether exclusions are justified, approved and visible in the audit file. For audit universe, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result indicates broad coverage of the defined population. A low result may be acceptable only where scope limitation, sampling strategy or risk-based exclusion is explicitly documented. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not equate broad coverage with high-quality audit evidence. Poorly defined populations can make the ratio misleading. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain audit universe, risk assessment, annual plan, scope memo, resource plan, engagement timetable, budget tracker, approval minutes and change log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Audit Universe Exception Rate; Audit Universe Completion Rate; Risk Assessment; Audit Plan; Audit Scope
terms.warning: Weak planning metrics can make later audit conclusions appear stronger than the scope supports. Always reconcile the metric to the approved scope and risk assessment. Coverage can be high while assurance remains weak if the wrong population is used.
terms.example: If 36 of 45 relevant audit universe items are included in the approved work programme, coverage is 80%. Document the reason for the nine exclusions.
terms.alignment: Aligned to risk-based planning and engagement planning principles used in IIA Global Internal Audit Standards, IAASB/ISA audit planning concepts, ACCA/ACA audit methodology and PMI-style delivery control.

terms.title: Audit Planning Audit Universe Exception Rate
terms.definition: This term measures how frequently deviations, errors, failures or non-compliant items were identified in the tested population. for the complete set of auditable entities, processes, systems, locations, risk themes and assurance objects from which the audit plan is built. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Audit Universe Exceptions / Audit Universe Items Tested
terms.components: Exceptions: deviations/errors; Items Tested: sample population. Define what counts as an exception before testing begins and separate severity levels where relevant.
terms.howToUse: Use it to identify the density of failures and to decide whether additional testing, root-cause analysis, management escalation or re-performance is required. For audit universe, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result signals potential control weakness, process instability, poor evidence quality or population issues. A low result supports, but does not prove, effective operation. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not compare exception rates across areas unless populations, sample design, criteria and severity thresholds are consistent. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain audit universe, risk assessment, annual plan, scope memo, resource plan, engagement timetable, budget tracker, approval minutes and change log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Audit Universe Coverage Ratio; Audit Universe Completion Rate; Risk Assessment; Audit Plan; Audit Scope
terms.warning: Weak planning metrics can make later audit conclusions appear stronger than the scope supports. Always reconcile the metric to the approved scope and risk assessment. Investigate whether exceptions are isolated, systemic, recurring, fraud-sensitive or evidence-related.
terms.example: If 7 exceptions are found in 70 tested audit universe items, the exception rate is 10%. Evaluate severity and root cause before concluding.
terms.alignment: Aligned to risk-based planning and engagement planning principles used in IIA Global Internal Audit Standards, IAASB/ISA audit planning concepts, ACCA/ACA audit methodology and PMI-style delivery control.

terms.title: Audit Planning Audit Universe Completion Rate
terms.definition: This term measures the proportion of planned audit activities, workpapers, tests or actions that have been completed. for the complete set of auditable entities, processes, systems, locations, risk themes and assurance objects from which the audit plan is built. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Completed Audit Universe Items / Planned Audit Universe Items
terms.components: Completed: finished items; Planned: audit plan population. Completed items should have evidence, preparer sign-off and review status, not merely a tick in a tracker.
terms.howToUse: Use it to monitor delivery progress and file readiness, but always combine it with quality review because completion alone does not prove sufficiency. For audit universe, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result shows planned work is substantially finished. A low result points to slippage, dependency gaps or weak audit project control. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not use completion rate as a proxy for audit quality or conclusion support. A completed test may still be weak, unsupported or incorrectly performed. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain audit universe, risk assessment, annual plan, scope memo, resource plan, engagement timetable, budget tracker, approval minutes and change log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Audit Universe Coverage Ratio; Audit Universe Exception Rate; Risk Assessment; Audit Plan; Audit Scope
terms.warning: Weak planning metrics can make later audit conclusions appear stronger than the scope supports. Always reconcile the metric to the approved scope and risk assessment.
terms.example: If 42 of 50 planned audit universe activities are complete and reviewed, completion is 84%. Unreviewed work should not be treated as final.
terms.alignment: Aligned to risk-based planning and engagement planning principles used in IIA Global Internal Audit Standards, IAASB/ISA audit planning concepts, ACCA/ACA audit methodology and PMI-style delivery control.

terms.title: Audit Planning Audit Universe Timeliness Rate
terms.definition: This term measures whether audit activities, requests, tests, reviews or actions were completed within the agreed deadline. for the complete set of auditable entities, processes, systems, locations, risk themes and assurance objects from which the audit plan is built. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Audit Universe Items Completed On Time / Audit Universe Items Due
terms.components: On Time: completed by deadline; Due: required items. Deadlines should come from the approved plan, request list, audit calendar or management action plan.
terms.howToUse: Use it to manage audit cadence, evidence requests, reporting deadlines and remediation promises. Late completion may indicate resource pressure, weak ownership or process resistance. For audit universe, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result shows work is moving to agreed timetable. A low result may indicate bottlenecks, management delay, reviewer backlog or unrealistic planning. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not reward speed where it compromises evidence quality, challenge, review or documentation. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain audit universe, risk assessment, annual plan, scope memo, resource plan, engagement timetable, budget tracker, approval minutes and change log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Audit Universe Coverage Ratio; Audit Universe Exception Rate; Risk Assessment; Audit Plan; Audit Scope
terms.warning: Weak planning metrics can make later audit conclusions appear stronger than the scope supports. Always reconcile the metric to the approved scope and risk assessment.
terms.example: If 18 of 24 due audit universe activities are completed by the agreed date, timeliness is 75%. Analyse delay causes and dependency ownership.
terms.alignment: Aligned to risk-based planning and engagement planning principles used in IIA Global Internal Audit Standards, IAASB/ISA audit planning concepts, ACCA/ACA audit methodology and PMI-style delivery control.

terms.title: Audit Planning Audit Universe Risk Score
terms.definition: This term combines assessed likelihood and impact to prioritise audit attention, escalation, remediation and review effort. for the complete set of auditable entities, processes, systems, locations, risk themes and assurance objects from which the audit plan is built. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Audit Universe Likelihood Score x Audit Universe Impact Score
terms.components: Likelihood: probability score; Impact: severity score. Likelihood and impact scales should be defined, consistently applied and reviewed when new evidence is identified.
terms.howToUse: Use it to prioritise audit work and management attention. The scoring should be based on defined criteria and reviewed when new evidence changes the risk view. For audit universe, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A higher score means greater urgency, review depth or escalation. A lower score should not remove audit attention if judgement, fraud indicators or regulatory sensitivity are present. For audit universe, the score should be supported by evidence, risk rationale and review notes.
terms.commonError: Do not treat a numeric score as a substitute for professional judgement. Scoring models must be calibrated, documented and reviewed. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain audit universe, risk assessment, annual plan, scope memo, resource plan, engagement timetable, budget tracker, approval minutes and change log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Audit Universe Coverage Ratio; Audit Universe Exception Rate; Risk Assessment; Audit Plan; Audit Scope
terms.warning: Weak planning metrics can make later audit conclusions appear stronger than the scope supports. Always reconcile the metric to the approved scope and risk assessment. Numeric scoring can create false precision; record the reasoning behind the score.
terms.example: If likelihood is scored 4 and impact is scored 5, the risk score is 20. Escalate according to the approved risk-rating matrix.
terms.alignment: Aligned to risk-based planning and engagement planning principles used in IIA Global Internal Audit Standards, IAASB/ISA audit planning concepts, ACCA/ACA audit methodology and PMI-style delivery control.

It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Audit Timeline Exceptions / Audit Timeline Items Tested
terms.components: Exceptions: deviations/errors; Items Tested: sample population. Define what counts as an exception before testing begins and separate severity levels where relevant.
terms.howToUse: Use it to identify the density of failures and to decide whether additional testing, root-cause analysis, management escalation or re-performance is required. For audit timeline, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result signals potential control weakness, process instability, poor evidence quality or population issues. A low result supports, but does not prove, effective operation. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not compare exception rates across areas unless populations, sample design, criteria and severity thresholds are consistent. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain audit universe, risk assessment, annual plan, scope memo, resource plan, engagement timetable, budget tracker, approval minutes and change log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Audit Timeline Coverage Ratio; Audit Timeline Completion Rate; Audit Budget; Audit Fieldwork; Audit Report
terms.warning: Weak planning metrics can make later audit conclusions appear stronger than the scope supports. Always reconcile the metric to the approved scope and risk assessment. Investigate whether exceptions are isolated, systemic, recurring, fraud-sensitive or evidence-related.
terms.example: If 7 exceptions are found in 70 tested audit timeline items, the exception rate is 10%. Evaluate severity and root cause before concluding.
terms.alignment: Aligned to risk-based planning and engagement planning principles used in IIA Global Internal Audit Standards, IAASB/ISA audit planning concepts, ACCA/ACA audit methodology and PMI-style delivery control.

terms.title: Audit Planning Audit Timeline Completion Rate
terms.definition: This term measures the proportion of planned audit activities, workpapers, tests or actions that have been completed. for the agreed sequencing of planning, fieldwork, reporting, review, management response and closure activities. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Completed Audit Timeline Items / Planned Audit Timeline Items
terms.components: Completed: finished items; Planned: audit plan population. Completed items should have evidence, preparer sign-off and review status, not merely a tick in a tracker.
terms.howToUse: Use it to monitor delivery progress and file readiness, but always combine it with quality review because completion alone does not prove sufficiency. For audit timeline, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result shows planned work is substantially finished. A low result points to slippage, dependency gaps or weak audit project control. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not use completion rate as a proxy for audit quality or conclusion support. A completed test may still be weak, unsupported or incorrectly performed. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain audit universe, risk assessment, annual plan, scope memo, resource plan, engagement timetable, budget tracker, approval minutes and change log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Audit Timeline Coverage Ratio; Audit Timeline Exception Rate; Audit Budget; Audit Fieldwork; Audit Report
terms.warning: Weak planning metrics can make later audit conclusions appear stronger than the scope supports. Always reconcile the metric to the approved scope and risk assessment.
terms.example: If 42 of 50 planned audit timeline activities are complete and reviewed, completion is 84%. Unreviewed work should not be treated as final.
terms.alignment: Aligned to risk-based planning and engagement planning principles used in IIA Global Internal Audit Standards, IAASB/ISA audit planning concepts, ACCA/ACA audit methodology and PMI-style delivery control.

terms.title: Audit Planning Audit Timeline Timeliness Rate
terms.definition: This term measures whether audit activities, requests, tests, reviews or actions were completed within the agreed deadline. for the agreed sequencing of planning, fieldwork, reporting, review, management response and closure activities. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Audit Timeline Items Completed On Time / Audit Timeline Items Due
terms.components: On Time: completed by deadline; Due: required items. Deadlines should come from the approved plan, request list, audit calendar or management action plan.
terms.howToUse: Use it to manage audit cadence, evidence requests, reporting deadlines and remediation promises. Late completion may indicate resource pressure, weak ownership or process resistance. For audit timeline, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result shows work is moving to agreed timetable. A low result may indicate bottlenecks, management delay, reviewer backlog or unrealistic planning. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not reward speed where it compromises evidence quality, challenge, review or documentation. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain audit universe, risk assessment, annual plan, scope memo, resource plan, engagement timetable, budget tracker, approval minutes and change log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Audit Timeline Coverage Ratio; Audit Timeline Exception Rate; Audit Budget; Audit Fieldwork; Audit Report
terms.warning: Weak planning metrics can make later audit conclusions appear stronger than the scope supports. Always reconcile the metric to the approved scope and risk assessment.
terms.example: If 18 of 24 due audit timeline activities are completed by the agreed date, timeliness is 75%. Analyse delay causes and dependency ownership.
terms.alignment: Aligned to risk-based planning and engagement planning principles used in IIA Global Internal Audit Standards, IAASB/ISA audit planning concepts, ACCA/ACA audit methodology and PMI-style delivery control.

terms.title: Audit Planning Audit Timeline Risk Score
terms.definition: This term combines assessed likelihood and impact to prioritise audit attention, escalation, remediation and review effort. for the agreed sequencing of planning, fieldwork, reporting, review, management response and closure activities. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Audit Timeline Likelihood Score x Audit Timeline Impact Score
terms.components: Likelihood: probability score; Impact: severity score. Likelihood and impact scales should be defined, consistently applied and reviewed when new evidence is identified.
terms.howToUse: Use it to prioritise audit work and management attention. The scoring should be based on defined criteria and reviewed when new evidence changes the risk view. For audit timeline, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A higher score means greater urgency, review depth or escalation. A lower score should not remove audit attention if judgement, fraud indicators or regulatory sensitivity are present. For audit timeline, the score should be supported by evidence, risk rationale and review notes.
terms.commonError: Do not treat a numeric score as a substitute for professional judgement. Scoring models must be calibrated, documented and reviewed. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain audit universe, risk assessment, annual plan, scope memo, resource plan, engagement timetable, budget tracker, approval minutes and change log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Audit Timeline Coverage Ratio; Audit Timeline Exception Rate; Audit Budget; Audit Fieldwork; Audit Report
terms.warning: Weak planning metrics can make later audit conclusions appear stronger than the scope supports. Always reconcile the metric to the approved scope and risk assessment. Numeric scoring can create false precision; record the reasoning behind the score.
terms.example: If likelihood is scored 4 and impact is scored 5, the risk score is 20. Escalate according to the approved risk-rating matrix.
terms.alignment: Aligned to risk-based planning and engagement planning principles used in IIA Global Internal Audit Standards, IAASB/ISA audit planning concepts, ACCA/ACA audit methodology and PMI-style delivery control.

terms.title: Materiality and Risk Planning Materiality Coverage Ratio
terms.definition: This term measures the proportion of the relevant audit population, requirement or work area that has been included in the audit scope, work programme or executed testing. for the materiality threshold used to design audit procedures and assess risks at financial statement or engagement level. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Planning Materiality Items Covered / Total Planning Materiality Items
terms.components: Covered: included in audit/testing; Total: audit population. Confirm that the denominator is the complete approved population and that exclusions are documented.
terms.howToUse: Use it to challenge whether the audit work covers the intended population and whether exclusions are justified, approved and visible in the audit file. For planning materiality, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result indicates broad coverage of the defined population. A low result may be acceptable only where scope limitation, sampling strategy or risk-based exclusion is explicitly documented. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not equate broad coverage with high-quality audit evidence. Poorly defined populations can make the ratio misleading. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain materiality paper, risk assessment, fraud brainstorming record, significant risk register, estimates schedule, audit strategy and partner/manager review notes. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Planning Materiality Exception Rate; Planning Materiality Completion Rate; Performance Materiality; Trivial Threshold; Aggregate Misstatement
terms.warning: Materiality and risk scores involve judgement. The calculation should support judgement, not replace it. Coverage can be high while assurance remains weak if the wrong population is used.
terms.example: If 36 of 45 relevant planning materiality items are included in the approved work programme, coverage is 80%. Document the reason for the nine exclusions.
terms.alignment: Aligned to materiality, professional judgement, fraud risk, significant risk and audit-risk concepts used in IAASB/ISA, ACCA/ACA and AICPA audit practice.

terms.title: Misstatements Classification Misstatement Coverage Ratio

terms.title: Internal Audit Delivery Audit Fieldwork Coverage Ratio
terms.definition: This term measures the proportion of the relevant audit population, requirement or work area that has been included in the audit scope, work programme or executed testing. for the evidence-gathering and testing stage of an audit engagement. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Audit Fieldwork Items Covered / Total Audit Fieldwork Items
terms.components: Covered: included in audit/testing; Total: audit population. Confirm that the denominator is the complete approved population and that exclusions are documented.
terms.howToUse: Use it to challenge whether the audit work covers the intended population and whether exclusions are justified, approved and visible in the audit file. For audit fieldwork, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result indicates broad coverage of the defined population. A low result may be acceptable only where scope limitation, sampling strategy or risk-based exclusion is explicitly documented. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not equate broad coverage with high-quality audit evidence. Poorly defined populations can make the ratio misleading. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain engagement charter, work programme, fieldwork notes, finding sheets, draft/final report, management action plan, review notes and close-out checklist. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Audit Fieldwork Exception Rate; Audit Fieldwork Completion Rate
terms.warning: Delivery metrics should not drive superficial closure. Audit quality depends on evidence, review, challenge and clear reporting. Coverage can be high while assurance remains weak if the wrong population is used.
terms.example: If 36 of 45 relevant audit fieldwork items are included in the approved work programme, coverage is 80%. Document the reason for the nine exclusions.
terms.alignment: Aligned to IIA standards for planning, performing, communicating results and monitoring progress, with project-management discipline for delivery control.

terms.title: Internal Audit Delivery Audit Fieldwork Exception Rate
terms.definition: This term measures how frequently deviations, errors, failures or non-compliant items were identified in the tested population. for the evidence-gathering and testing stage of an audit engagement. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Audit Fieldwork Exceptions / Audit Fieldwork Items Tested
terms.components: Exceptions: deviations/errors; Items Tested: sample population. Define what counts as an exception before testing begins and separate severity levels where relevant.
terms.howToUse: Use it to identify the density of failures and to decide whether additional testing, root-cause analysis, management escalation or re-performance is required. For audit fieldwork, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result signals potential control weakness, process instability, poor evidence quality or population issues. A low result supports, but does not prove, effective operation. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not compare exception rates across areas unless populations, sample design, criteria and severity thresholds are consistent. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain engagement charter, work programme, fieldwork notes, finding sheets, draft/final report, management action plan, review notes and close-out checklist. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Audit Fieldwork Coverage Ratio; Audit Fieldwork Completion Rate
terms.warning: Delivery metrics should not drive superficial closure. Audit quality depends on evidence, review, challenge and clear reporting. Investigate whether exceptions are isolated, systemic, recurring, fraud-sensitive or evidence-related.
terms.example: If 7 exceptions are found in 70 tested audit fieldwork items, the exception rate is 10%. Evaluate severity and root cause before concluding.
terms.alignment: Aligned to IIA standards for planning, performing, communicating results and monitoring progress, with project-management discipline for delivery control.

terms.evidence: Retain engagement charter, work programme, fieldwork notes, finding sheets, draft/final report, management action plan, review notes and close-out checklist. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.

terms.title: Audit Quality and Assurance Evidence Sufficiency Coverage Ratio
terms.definition: This term measures the proportion of the relevant audit population, requirement or work area that has been included in the audit scope, work programme or executed testing. for whether the quantity and coverage of evidence is enough to support the conclusion. terms.formula: Evidence Sufficiency Items Covered / Total Evidence Sufficiency Items

terms.howToUse: Use it to challenge whether the audit work covers the intended population and whether exclusions are justified, approved and visible in the audit file. terms.interpretation: A high result indicates broad coverage of the defined population. terms.commonError: Do not equate broad coverage with high-quality audit evidence. Poorly defined populations can make the ratio misleading. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain quality review notes, evidence sufficiency assessment, assurance map, reliance evaluation, independence/objectivity checks, competence record, audit committee paper and external auditor coordination log. terms.related: Evidence Sufficiency Exception Rate; Evidence Sufficiency Completion Rate
terms.warning: Reliance and coordination metrics must preserve independence, objectivity and clear responsibility for conclusions. Coverage can be high while assurance remains weak if the wrong population is used.
terms.example: If 36 of 45 relevant evidence sufficiency items are included in the approved work programme, coverage is 80%. Document the reason for the nine exclusions.
terms.alignment: Aligned to IIA quality, independence, objectivity and competence principles, external audit quality-management expectations, assurance mapping and FRC audit committee expectations.

terms.title: Audit Quality and Assurance Evidence Sufficiency Exception Rate

For evidence sufficiency, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result signals potential control weakness, process instability, poor evidence quality or population issues. A low result supports, but does not prove, effective operation. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not compare exception rates across areas unless populations, sample design, criteria and severity thresholds are consistent. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain quality review notes, evidence sufficiency assessment, assurance map, reliance evaluation, independence/objectivity checks, competence record, audit committee paper and external auditor coordination log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Evidence Sufficiency Coverage Ratio; Evidence Sufficiency Completion Rate

terms.alignment: Aligned to IIA quality, independence, objectivity and competence principles, external audit quality-management expectations, assurance mapping and FRC audit committee expectations.

terms.formula: Assurance Map Likelihood Score x Assurance Map Impact Score
terms.components: Likelihood: probability score; Impact: severity score. Likelihood and impact scales should be defined, consistently applied and reviewed when new evidence is identified.
terms.howToUse: Use it to prioritise audit work and management attention. The scoring should be based on defined criteria and reviewed when new evidence changes the risk view. For assurance map, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A higher score means greater urgency, review depth or escalation. A lower score should not remove audit attention if judgement, fraud indicators or regulatory sensitivity are present. terms.title: Audit Quality and Assurance Reliance Assessment Coverage Ratio
terms.definition: This term measures the proportion of the relevant audit population, requirement or work area that has been included in the audit scope, work programme or executed testing. for the assessment of whether another party’s work can be used, and to what extent, in supporting audit conclusions. It helps practitioners convert audit work into a controlled, reviewable measure without removing the need for professional judgement.
terms.formula: Reliance Assessment Items Covered / Total Reliance Assessment Items
terms.components: Covered: included in audit/testing; Total: audit population. Confirm that the denominator is the complete approved population and that exclusions are documented.
terms.howToUse: Use it to challenge whether the audit work covers the intended population and whether exclusions are justified, approved and visible in the audit file. For reliance assessment, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result indicates broad coverage of the defined population. A low result may be acceptable only where scope limitation, sampling strategy or risk-based exclusion is explicitly documented. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not equate broad coverage with high-quality audit evidence. Poorly defined populations can make the ratio misleading. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain quality review notes, evidence sufficiency assessment, assurance map, reliance evaluation, independence/objectivity checks, competence record, audit committee paper and external auditor coordination log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Reliance Assessment Exception Rate; Reliance Assessment Completion Rate
terms.warning: Reliance and coordination metrics must preserve independence, objectivity and clear responsibility for conclusions. Coverage can be high while assurance remains weak if the wrong population is used.
terms.example: If 36 of 45 relevant reliance assessment items are included in the approved work programme, coverage is 80%. Document the reason for the nine exclusions.
terms.alignment: Aligned to IIA quality, independence, objectivity and competence principles, external audit quality-management expectations, assurance mapping and FRC audit committee expectations.

terms.title: Audit Quality and Assurance Reliance Assessment Exception Rate
terms.definition: This term measures how frequently deviations, errors, failures or non-compliant items were identified in the tested population. for the assessment of whether another party’s work can be used, and to what extent, in supporting audit conclusions. terms.components: Exceptions: deviations/errors; Items Tested: sample population. Define what counts as an exception before testing begins and separate severity levels where relevant.
terms.howToUse: Use it to identify the density of failures and to decide whether additional testing, root-cause analysis, management escalation or re-performance is required. For reliance assessment, apply the measure during planning, fieldwork review, reporting or follow-up as appropriate, and keep the result traceable to the audit file.
terms.interpretation: A high result signals potential control weakness, process instability, poor evidence quality or population issues. A low result supports, but does not prove, effective operation. Interpret the result alongside severity, materiality, scope limitations and evidence quality.
terms.commonError: Do not compare exception rates across areas unless populations, sample design, criteria and severity thresholds are consistent. Avoid using the number without reading the underlying exceptions, reviewer comments and management responses.
terms.evidence: Retain quality review notes, evidence sufficiency assessment, assurance map, reliance evaluation, independence/objectivity checks, competence record, audit committee paper and external auditor coordination log. The evidence should identify preparer, reviewer, date, source population, exceptions and conclusion.
terms.related: Reliance Assessment Coverage Ratio; Reliance Assessment Completion Rate
terms.warning: Reliance and coordination metrics must preserve independence, objectivity and clear responsibility for conclusions. Investigate whether exceptions are isolated, systemic, recurring, fraud-sensitive or evidence-related.
terms.example: If 7 exceptions are found in 70 tested reliance assessment items, the exception rate is 10%. Evaluate severity and root cause before concluding.
terms.alignment: Aligned to IIA quality, independence, objectivity and competence principles, external audit quality-management expectations, assurance mapping and FRC audit committee expectations.

terms.title: Audit Quality and Assurance Reliance Assessment Completion Rate

terms.evidence: Retain quality review notes, evidence sufficiency assessment, assurance map, reliance evaluation, independence/objectivity checks, competence record, audit committee paper and external auditor coordination log. terms.title: Board Composition Board Independence Ratio
terms.definition: Board Independence ratio measures the proportion, structural share or relative presence of the governance item within the relevant population. for the extent to which board members can exercise objective judgement without relationships, tenure, ownership or executive responsibilities that may impair independence.. It is a governance diagnostic measure, not a stand-alone conclusion.
terms.formula: Board Independence Count / Total Relevant Count
terms.components: Count: selected governance item; Total: relevant population. Define the relevant population before calculation. Count only items meeting the approved definition.
terms.howToUse: Use it during board composition review, annual report governance drafting, director independence assessment and nomination committee planning. Use the ratio to establish the structural position before making a qualitative judgement. It should inform governance challenge; it should not replace board judgement.
terms.interpretation: A high or low result is not automatically good or bad. Interpret it against governance objective, board composition, ownership structure, committee remit and organisational complexity.
terms.commonError: Do not treat the percentage as a judgement of effectiveness. Ratios can hide quality, independence, skill, influence or behavioural issues.
terms.evidence: board composition schedule; director register; independence assessment; skills matrix; appointment letters; tenure schedule; nomination committee papers; annual report governance draft. Confirm numerator and denominator populations are defined consistently.
terms.related: Coverage; Timeliness; Breach Rate; Effectiveness Score; governance dashboard; board pack metric.
terms.warning: Ratios support governance diagnosis but do not prove independence, competence, fairness or quality of challenge.
terms.example: If board independence count is 4 and the relevant population is 10, the ratio is 40%. The practitioner then explains what the ratio means for board oversight, not merely the percentage.
terms.alignment: Aligned to UK Corporate Governance Code board leadership, composition, independence, succession and evaluation principles; also relevant to ICAEW/ACCA/CIMA governance and ethical leadership expectations. This is professional alignment, not endorsement or certification by any body.

terms.title: Board Composition Board Independence Coverage
terms.definition: Board Independence coverage measures whether required governance items are documented, approved, monitored or otherwise covered by the governance framework. for the extent to which board members can exercise objective judgement without relationships, tenure, ownership or executive responsibilities that may impair independence.. It is a governance diagnostic measure, not a stand-alone conclusion.
terms.formula: Board Independence Items Covered / Board Independence Items Required
terms.components: Covered: documented/approved/monitored; Required: governance requirement. Map required items to documented owner, approval status, monitoring status and review frequency.
terms.howToUse: Use it during board composition review, annual report governance drafting, director independence assessment and nomination committee planning. Use coverage to verify whether the governance requirement exists in documented and operational form. It is useful for gap analysis, policy mapping and board pack assurance.
terms.interpretation: High coverage suggests the topic is formally embedded. Low coverage indicates missing governance documentation, weak ownership or insufficient monitoring.
terms.commonError: Do not count documents that are outdated, unapproved, unknown to users or not operating in practice.

packs.label: Merixa Risk Management Practitioner Glossary v2

terms.title: Enterprise Market Exposure Ratio
terms.definition: Enterprise Market Exposure Ratio is a proportional measure showing how much of the relevant risk exposure belongs to the selected risk class or source. It is applied to enterprise market within enterprise risk appetite and exposure management and should be interpreted with the relevant risk appetite, time horizon, confidence level, portfolio scope or operating context.
terms.formula: Market Exposure / Total Risk Exposure
terms.components: Market Exposure: measured exposure; Total Risk Exposure: aggregate exposure base Data control: Confirm numerator and denominator use the same population, period and measurement basis; validate multiplicative drivers independently because small assumption errors can compound.
terms.howToUse: Use during risk appetite assessment, enterprise risk mapping, limit-setting, exposure monitoring and board or committee risk reporting. Compare current exposure to approved appetite and explain movements, breaches and headroom.
terms.interpretation: Interpret trend, level and threshold together. A single-period result rarely provides enough evidence; use movement, volatility, concentration, severity and management response to form a practitioner conclusion.
terms.commonError: Using the metric without confirming the data population, period, scope and owner. Comparing ratios where denominators differ or where the population has changed between periods.
terms.evidence: Evidence should include source data extract, reporting date, responsible owner, calculation workbook or system report, threshold/appetite reference, review notes, exceptions, approvals and version history. Add approved risk appetite statement, limit register, exposure register, breach log and committee reporting pack.
terms.related: Same measurement family entries: 002, 003, 004, 005. Related concepts: risk appetite statement; risk capacity; limit utilisation; breach log; exposure register.
terms.warning: Risk metrics support professional judgement; they do not replace risk ownership, management challenge, board oversight or specialist advice where required.
terms.example: Example: calculate the metric for the current period, compare it with threshold and prior trend, then document the driver, judgement, owner action and review conclusion.
terms.alignment: CRMA and COSO ERM-style risk governance: risk appetite, risk capacity, risk ownership, monitoring and escalation. This is professional alignment language only; it does not imply certification, endorsement, audit opinion or regulatory approval.

terms.title: Enterprise Market Limit Utilisation
terms.definition: Enterprise Market Limit Utilisation is a measure of how much of an approved risk appetite, risk limit or management threshold has been consumed. It is applied to enterprise market within enterprise risk appetite and exposure management and should be interpreted with the relevant risk appetite, time horizon, confidence level, portfolio scope or operating context.
terms.formula: Market Exposure / Approved Market Limit
terms.components: Exposure: measured Market amount; Limit: approved appetite or risk limit Data control: Confirm numerator and denominator use the same population, period and measurement basis; validate multiplicative drivers independently because small assumption errors can compound.
terms.howToUse: Use during risk appetite assessment, enterprise risk mapping, limit-setting, exposure monitoring and board or committee risk reporting. Compare current exposure to approved appetite and explain movements, breaches and headroom. The practitioner should document the approved limit owner, limit date, delegated authority and escalation route before treating the result as actionable.
terms.interpretation: Higher utilisation means less remaining capacity under the approved limit. High utilisation may be acceptable if planned and temporary, but it requires explanation, ownership and monitoring. Persistent high utilisation suggests appetite pressure or limit design issues.
terms.commonError: Using the metric without confirming the data population, period, scope and owner. Treating a limit as current without confirming approval date, delegated authority and whether the limit still reflects strategy and risk capacity.
terms.evidence: Evidence should include source data extract, reporting date, responsible owner, calculation workbook or system report, threshold/appetite reference, review notes, exceptions, approvals and version history. Add approved risk appetite statement, limit register, exposure register, breach log and committee reporting pack.
terms.related: Same measurement family entries: 001, 003, 004, 005. Related concepts: risk appetite statement; risk capacity; limit utilisation; breach log; exposure register.
terms.warning: Risk metrics support professional judgement; they do not replace risk ownership, management challenge, board oversight or specialist advice where required.
terms.example: Example: exposure of GBP 8m against an approved GBP 10m limit gives 80% utilisation. If the internal warning level is 75%, the pack should explain driver, owner action and expected resolution.
terms.alignment: CRMA and COSO ERM-style risk governance: risk appetite, risk capacity, risk ownership, monitoring and escalation. This is professional alignment language only; it does not imply certification, endorsement, audit opinion or regulatory approval.

terms.title: Enterprise Market Limit Headroom
terms.definition: Enterprise Market Limit Headroom is the estimated exposure outstanding at the point of default, including drawn balances and relevant undrawn or contingent exposures. In Merixa work, use it as a structured risk measure within enterprise risk appetite and exposure management, supported by source data, assumptions and management-approved thresholds.
terms.formula: Approved Market Limit - Market Exposure
terms.components: Limit: approved threshold; Exposure: current measured amount Data control: Document direction of variance so favourable and adverse movements are not reversed; validate multiplicative drivers independently because small assumption errors can compound.

terms.title: Historical Simulation VaR
terms.definition: Historical Simulation VaR is a downside loss estimate at a defined confidence level and holding period. It supports risk-limit setting and stress comparison, but it is not a worst-case loss measure. In Merixa work, use it as a structured risk measure within market risk measurement and limit monitoring, supported by source data, assumptions and management-approved thresholds.
terms.formula: Percentile Loss from Historical P&L Distribution
terms.components: Historical P&L: ordered changes; Percentile: confidence level Data control: Retain the ordered distribution, confidence level and holding period.
terms.howToUse: Use in market risk monitoring, trading exposure review, treasury sensitivity analysis and VaR or stress reporting. Tie the measure to approved limits, portfolio scope, confidence level and holding period. Use it with scenario commentary and stress context; do not report the number without assumptions, exclusions and known model limitations.
terms.interpretation: VaR-type outputs summarise threshold loss under specified assumptions. They do not show the size of losses beyond the threshold and can understate tail risk if distributions, correlations or volatility assumptions are unstable.
terms.commonError: Using the metric without confirming the data population, period, scope and owner. Reporting model output as fact without assumptions, validation, backtesting, sensitivity and limitation notes.
terms.evidence: Evidence should include source data extract, reporting date, responsible owner, calculation workbook or system report, threshold/appetite reference, review notes, exceptions, approvals and version history. Add position file, price/rate source, volatility and correlation input, VaR/stress configuration, sensitivity report and limit report.
terms.related: Same measurement family entries: 137, 138, 139, 140. Related concepts: VaR; expected shortfall; sensitivity; stress loss; volatility; limit utilisation.
terms.warning: Market risk model outputs can be materially wrong during regime shifts, illiquidity or correlation breakdown. Always state confidence level, holding period, portfolio scope and limitations.
terms.example: Example: a 99% one-day VaR of GBP 1.2m means the model estimates losses should exceed GBP 1.2m on about 1% of days under its assumptions. It does not cap the loss.

In Merixa work, use it as a structured risk measure within market risk measurement and limit monitoring, supported by source data, assumptions and management-approved thresholds.
terms.formula: 0.5 x Convexity x Yield Change^2 x Bond Value
terms.components: Convexity: curvature; Yield Change: rate shock; Bond Value: exposure Data control: Validate multiplicative drivers independently because small assumption errors can compound.
terms.howToUse: Use in market risk monitoring, trading exposure review, treasury sensitivity analysis and VaR or stress reporting. Tie the measure to approved limits, portfolio scope, confidence level and holding period.
terms.interpretation: Interpret trend, level and threshold together. A single-period result rarely provides enough evidence; use movement, volatility, concentration, severity and management response to form a practitioner conclusion.
terms.commonError: Using the metric without confirming the data population, period, scope and owner.
terms.evidence: Evidence should include source data extract, reporting date, responsible owner, calculation workbook or system report, threshold/appetite reference, review notes, exceptions, approvals and version history. Add position file, price/rate source, volatility and correlation input, VaR/stress configuration, sensitivity report and limit report.

terms.title: Capital Risk Shareholder Value Headroom

terms.interpretation: Positive headroom indicates remaining capacity before breach. Declining headroom is an early-warning signal. Negative headroom indicates breach or overrun and should trigger escalation according to governance rules.
terms.commonError: Using the metric without confirming the data population, period, scope and owner. Using stale ratings, unsupported overlays or collateral values that have not been refreshed.

terms.title: Control Design Entity-Level Coverage Ratio
terms.definition: A measure of whether the required entity-level control population has been designed or implemented against the agreed control baseline. It answers whether the necessary controls exist before judging whether they work.
terms.formula: Entity-Level Controls Implemented / Entity-Level Controls Required

terms.formula: Annual Exceptions / Annual Control Checks
terms.components: Exceptions: failed checks; Control Checks: performed checks Additional data discipline: confirm source system, reporting period, process, control owner, population, test basis, preparer, reviewer and version used.
terms.howToUse: Use during periodic control operation review. Compare actual performance against the control calendar, test plan or operating requirement and identify gaps by control owner, process and period. Use exception rate to prioritise root-cause analysis, remediation ownership and whether a design change is needed.
terms.interpretation: A rising exception rate indicates weaker execution, control fatigue, policy non-compliance, system gaps or poor review discipline. A low exception rate is useful only where the test population is complete and testing criteria are robust.
terms.commonError: Treating every exception as equally important without considering control objective, financial reporting impact and fraud exposure. Suppressing exceptions by narrowing the test population or changing definitions after testing.
terms.evidence: Evidence should include the control description, owner, frequency, population, sample selection, test criteria, preparer, reviewer, date performed, exception log and final conclusion. Add control calendar, operating evidence, period close packs, workflow approvals and proof that late or missing controls were followed up.
terms.related: Same control family entries: 071, 072, 074, 075. Control objective; risk-control matrix; control owner; evidence standard; exception log; remediation tracker; testing plan. Related: coverage ratio, timeliness rate and defect density for the same control population.
terms.alignment: COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring as relevant.

terms.title: Control Operation Annual Timeliness Rate
terms.definition: A measure of whether annual control activities were completed within the approved deadline or control cadence. It is important where late operation reduces the value of the control even if it was eventually completed.
terms.formula: Annual Activities Completed On Time / Annual Activities Due
terms.components: On-Time: completed by deadline; Due: scheduled activities Additional data discipline: confirm source system, reporting period, process, control owner, population, test basis, preparer, reviewer and version used.
terms.howToUse: Use during periodic control operation review. Compare actual performance against the control calendar, test plan or operating requirement and identify gaps by control owner, process and period. Use timeliness to assess whether the control was available at the point of risk, not merely whether it was completed eventually.
terms.interpretation: A strong timeliness rate supports control cadence and accountability. Late operation can undermine preventive and detective controls because the risk may already have crystallised before review.
terms.commonError: Marking late evidence as on time because it was produced before the review meeting rather than by the control deadline. Ignoring controls that are technically completed but too late to prevent or detect the underlying risk.
terms.evidence: Evidence should include the control description, owner, frequency, population, sample selection, test criteria, preparer, reviewer, date performed, exception log and final conclusion. Add control calendar, operating evidence, period close packs, workflow approvals and proof that late or missing controls were followed up.
terms.related: Same control family entries: 071, 072, 073, 075. Control objective; risk-control matrix; control owner; evidence standard; exception log; remediation tracker; testing plan.
terms.alignment: COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring as relevant.

terms.title: Control Operation Annual Defect Density
terms.definition: A concentration measure showing how many annual defects were found in the tested population. It helps distinguish isolated exceptions from systemic weakness or poor control design.
terms.formula: Annual Defects / Annual Items Tested
terms.components: Defects: control weaknesses; Items Tested: sampled/tested items Additional data discipline: confirm source system, reporting period, process, control owner, population, test basis, preparer, reviewer and version used.
terms.howToUse: Use during periodic control operation review. Compare actual performance against the control calendar, test plan or operating requirement and identify gaps by control owner, process and period. Use defect density when comparing areas with different sample sizes or transaction volumes, but avoid using it without severity assessment.
terms.interpretation: Higher defect density suggests concentrated weakness or systemic process failure. Compare against prior periods, control type and severity; do not treat all defects as equal.
terms.commonError: Comparing defect density between processes without normalising for sample size, complexity and risk profile. Using defect counts without root-cause analysis or severity classification.
terms.evidence: Evidence should include the control description, owner, frequency, population, sample selection, test criteria, preparer, reviewer, date performed, exception log and final conclusion. terms.title: Control Operation High-Risk Coverage Ratio
terms.definition: A measure of whether the required high-risk control population has been designed or implemented against the agreed control baseline. It answers whether the necessary controls exist before judging whether they work.
terms.formula: High-Risk Controls Implemented / High-Risk Controls Required
terms.components: Implemented: active controls; Required: control design baseline Additional data discipline: confirm source system, reporting period, process, control owner, population, test basis, preparer, reviewer and version used.
terms.howToUse: Use during periodic control operation review. Compare actual performance against the control calendar, test plan or operating requirement and identify gaps by control owner, process and period. Coverage should be assessed before testing pass/fail results because an incomplete population can make later metrics misleading.
terms.interpretation: Higher coverage usually indicates stronger design completeness. Low coverage may indicate unaddressed risks, missing controls, incomplete control libraries or unclear ownership. High coverage does not prove control quality or operating effectiveness.
terms.commonError: Counting a control as covered when it is only drafted, not implemented or not assigned to an accountable owner. Using coverage as evidence of effectiveness. A control can exist and still fail.
terms.evidence: Evidence should include the control description, owner, frequency, population, sample selection, test criteria, preparer, reviewer, date performed, exception log and final conclusion. Add control calendar, operating evidence, period close packs, workflow approvals and proof that late or missing controls were followed up.

terms.warning: Use this metric as a management and practitioner control measure. It does not constitute audit assurance, certification or legal/regulatory conclusion.

terms.title: Control Operation High-Risk Pass Rate
terms.definition: A measure of the proportion of high-risk tests that passed the defined design or operating test criteria. It supports evaluation of whether controls are performing as intended within the tested population.
terms.formula: Passed High-Risk Tests / Total High-Risk Tests
terms.components: Passed Tests: effective results; Total Tests: tested population Additional data discipline: confirm source system, reporting period, process, control owner, population, test basis, preparer, reviewer and version used.
terms.howToUse: Use during periodic control operation review. Compare actual performance against the control calendar, test plan or operating requirement and identify gaps by control owner, process and period. Use pass rate to summarise test outcomes, but retain the exception log and sample details because pass rate alone does not explain severity.
terms.interpretation: A high pass rate suggests the tested control population largely met criteria. A low pass rate signals operating weakness, poor evidence, unclear procedures or sample-selection issues. Material exceptions require qualitative assessment even where the overall pass rate appears acceptable.
terms.commonError: Reporting pass rate without explaining exception severity, sample basis and whether failed items are repeat issues. Allowing control owners to self-mark pass results without review or evidence traceability.
terms.evidence: Evidence should include the control description, owner, frequency, population, sample selection, test criteria, preparer, reviewer, date performed, exception log and final conclusion. Track whether deficiencies are identified, classified, assigned, remediated, validated and closed with evidence rather than only marked as actioned. terms.components: Defects: control weaknesses; Items Tested: sampled/tested items Additional data discipline: confirm source system, reporting period, process, control owner, population, test basis, preparer, reviewer and version used.

terms.title: Deficiency Deficiency Validation Coverage Ratio

terms.title: Parent Ownership Percentage
terms.definition: The measured ownership interest in Parent, used to support control assessment, consolidation scoping, NCI allocation and group structure documentation.
terms.formula: Shares Held in Parent / Total Shares of Parent
terms.components: Shares Held: direct or indirect holding; Total Shares: issued voting/equity shares Additional data discipline: confirm source system, reporting period, entity, currency, ownership basis, preparer, reviewer and version used.
terms.howToUse: Use during group structure review, consolidation scoping and NCI allocation. Reconcile to legal registers, acquisition documents and the group structure chart before relying on the percentage in consolidation schedules.
terms.interpretation: A higher percentage is generally better, but only if the denominator is complete and appropriate. Investigate ratios near 100% where the underlying population may be incomplete or excluded.
terms.commonError: Using legal shareholding as a substitute for control assessment without considering rights, power and variable returns. Applying the wrong percentage to post-acquisition profit, NCI or reserves.
terms.evidence: source trial balance or reporting pack; consolidation workbook reference; preparer and reviewer sign-off; legal entity register; share certificates or acquisition agreements; group structure chart.
terms.alignment: IFRS 10 consolidation and control discipline.

terms.title: Parent Effective Ownership
terms.definition: The indirect economic ownership in Parent after tracing holdings through the chain of ownership rather than looking only at the immediate parent.
terms.formula: Direct Ownership x Indirect Chain Ownership
terms.components: Direct Ownership: immediate holding; Indirect Chain: product of intermediate holdings Additional data discipline: confirm source system, reporting period, entity, currency, ownership basis, preparer, reviewer and version used.
terms.howToUse: Use during group structure review, consolidation scoping and NCI allocation. Reconcile to legal registers, acquisition documents and the group structure chart before relying on the percentage in consolidation schedules.
terms.interpretation: Interpret in the context of materiality, reporting purpose, evidence quality and whether the measure is being used for calculation, control, disclosure or review.
terms.commonError: Using legal shareholding as a substitute for control assessment without considering rights, power and variable returns. Applying the wrong percentage to post-acquisition profit, NCI or reserves.
terms.evidence: source trial balance or reporting pack; consolidation workbook reference; preparer and reviewer sign-off; legal entity register; share certificates or acquisition agreements; group structure chart.
terms.alignment: IFRS 10 consolidation and control discipline.

terms.title: Parent Reporting Pack Completion
terms.definition: A completeness measure for the Parent reporting pack, showing whether the required group reporting fields have been populated for consolidation.
terms.formula: Completed Parent Pack Fields / Required Parent Pack Fields
terms.components: Completed Fields: populated fields; Required Fields: group pack fields Additional data discipline: confirm source system, reporting period, entity, currency, ownership basis, preparer, reviewer and version used.
terms.howToUse: Use during entity pack intake and close control. The associate should identify incomplete pack fields or unmapped trial balance lines before the partner reviews consolidation outputs.
terms.interpretation: A higher percentage is generally better, but only if the denominator is complete and appropriate. Investigate ratios near 100% where the underlying population may be incomplete or excluded.
terms.commonError: Treating a completed field as evidence that the underlying amount is correct. Leaving unmapped trial balance lines in suspense or forcing them into generic accounts.
terms.evidence: source trial balance or reporting pack; consolidation workbook reference; preparer and reviewer sign-off.

terms.title: IFRS 3 business combination Disclosure Completion

terms.title: Accounting equation
terms.definition: The fundamental financial statement relationship that total recognised assets equal total recognised liabilities plus equity.
terms.formula: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
terms.components: Assets: recognised resources. Liabilities: present obligations. Equity: residual interest. Data should be taken from controlled reporting sources: trial balance, consolidation workbook, subledger, note schedule, contract register, tax schedule, valuation support or approved management estimate, as applicable.
terms.howToUse: Use in the preparation file to calculate the relevant financial statement amount, perform analytical review and support the final disclosure or primary statement presentation.
terms.interpretation: The calculated amount should agree to the financial statement architecture and be explainable through source records, accounting policy and period movement analysis.
terms.commonError: Applying the calculation without confirming scope, period, data source, accounting policy and whether the result is before or after tax, before or after elimination, or continuing versus total operations.
terms.evidence: final trial balance or consolidation workbook.
terms.related: 154 Effective interest rate equation
terms.alignment: Professionally aligned to IFRS financial statement preparation and ACCA/CIMA reporting discipline. This Merixa term is a practitioner aid and is not a substitute for formal accounting judgement, audit opinion or external technical advice.

terms.title: Net assets
terms.definition: The residual value of recognised assets after deducting recognised liabilities at the reporting date.
terms.formula: Net assets = Total assets - Total liabilities
terms.components: Total assets: current + non-current assets. Total liabilities: current + non-current liabilities. Data should be taken from controlled reporting sources: trial balance, consolidation workbook, subledger, note schedule, contract register, tax schedule, valuation support or approved management estimate, as applicable.

packs.label: Merixa Financial Analysis Practitioner Glossary v2

terms.title: 001 - Holding Period Return
terms.definition: Holding Period Return is a measure of profit, cash flow, income or value movement relative to invested capital, price, equity or another base. It is used in return measurement, compounding, discounting, investment appraisal and time-value-of-money analysis. The term is meaningful only when the numerator, denominator, period, population and purpose are clearly defined.
terms.formula: (Ending Value - Beginning Value + Income) / Beginning Value
terms.components: Ending Value: closing price/value; Beginning Value: opening price/value; Income: dividends, interest or distributions Confirm numerator and denominator use the same period, population, currency and scope; document the direction of movement so favourable and adverse results are not reversed; reconcile each added component to the source schedule or model.
terms.howToUse: Use this term when evaluating investment returns, discounting cash flows, comparing compounding conventions, building investment cases or checking whether valuation and finance models use consistent time-value assumptions.
terms.interpretation: Interpret the result against prior periods, forecast, budget, peers, sector norms and the organisation’s business model. A higher number is not automatically favourable; for example, growth can be low-quality, turnover can reflect underinvestment, and high yield may signal risk.
terms.commonError: Mixing periods, currencies or populations. Using unaudited, unreconciled or stale data without labelling limitations. Treating a single metric as a conclusion rather than a diagnostic indicator.
terms.evidence: Source cash-flow schedule, price/value data, income records, discount/interest-rate basis, compounding convention and calculation workbook. Keep evidence of preparer, reviewer, date, source system and any manual adjustment.
terms.related: NPV; IRR; Discount Factor; Required Return; WACC; Real Return; Annualised Return; Required Return
terms.alignment: CFA-style investment mathematics, ACCA/CIMA finance and corporate finance appraisal discipline.

terms.title: 002 - Price Return
terms.definition: Price Return is a measure of profit, cash flow, income or value movement relative to invested capital, price, equity or another base. It is used in return measurement, compounding, discounting, investment appraisal and time-value-of-money analysis. The term is meaningful only when the numerator, denominator, period, population and purpose are clearly defined.

terms.definition: An annualised or periodised estimate of recurring revenue based on the most recent period. It is a directional management indicator, not a substitute for a properly modelled forecast.
terms.howToUse: Use it as a quick directional view of recurring revenue when a full forecast is not yet updated. Pair it with seasonality and known one-off adjustments.
terms.interpretation: Interpret the percentage together with absolute amounts. A good-looking ratio can hide a small base, one-off movement, denominator distortion or classification change.
terms.commonError: Using a small, zero or inconsistent denominator without warning. Annualising a one-off, seasonal or abnormal period without adjustment.
terms.evidence: source data extract; calculation workbook; reconciliation to management pack; approved budget or forecast file; assumption register; sales ledger or CRM extract; pricing/discount schedule.
terms.related:
Run-rate value; annualised revenue run rate; rolling average; forecast variance.
Example wording / mini-example: Mini-example: if the latest month recurring revenue is £100k and the annualisation factor is 12, the simple run rate is £1.2m before seasonality or one-offs.
terms.alignment: Professional use: apply consistently with the agreed management reporting basis, source data, assumptions and review cadence.
terms.title: Recurring revenue Run Rate

terms.formula: (Actual Recurring revenue - Comparator Recurring revenue) / Comparator Recurring revenue
terms.components: Actual Recurring revenue: measured result; Comparator Recurring revenue: budget, forecast or prior period
terms.definition: A variance expressed relative to a comparator. It normalises movement so that management can compare the size of changes across different accounts, sites, products or reporting lines.
terms.howToUse: Use it to rank movements by relative size after absolute amounts have been reviewed. Always calculate it against a meaningful, non-zero comparator.
terms.interpretation: A positive or negative variance is not automatically favourable or adverse. Interpret by the nature of the metric: higher revenue may be favourable; higher cost, debt days or error rates may be adverse.
terms.commonError: Treating the variance as the explanation rather than investigating its drivers. Using a small, zero or inconsistent denominator without warning.
terms.evidence: source data extract; calculation workbook; reconciliation to management pack; sales ledger or CRM extract; pricing/discount schedule.
terms.related:
Absolute variance; budget variance; forecast variance; variance contribution percentage.
Example wording / mini-example: Mini-example: if actual is 110 and comparator is 100, the variance percentage is 10%.
terms.alignment: ACCA/CIMA management accounting alignment: useful for planning, control, variance investigation and management decision support.
terms.title: Recurring revenue Variance Percentage

terms.formula: Actual Direct material Result - Standard Direct material Result
terms.components: Actual Result: measured outcome; Standard Result: allowed standard Data should be drawn from controlled operational, costing, HR, service, production, finance or KPI sources with period cut-off confirmed.
terms.definition: The overall difference between the actual and standard result for direct material. It is a first diagnostic measure before decomposing the movement into price, usage, mix, efficiency, volume or planning drivers.
terms.howToUse: Use during monthly performance review, budget holder meetings and operational diagnostics. Start with the total variance, then drill down to the driver responsible before assigning actions.
terms.interpretation: A favourable or adverse result depends on the metric direction. A positive revenue variance is usually favourable; a positive cost variance is usually adverse unless the formula is explicitly reversed.
terms.commonError: calling a variance favourable or adverse without checking metric direction; mixing fixed budget, flexed budget and revised standard baselines.
terms.evidence: approved formula definition; source data extract; reconciliation to reporting pack; owner review sign-off; actual results; budget or standard file; flexed/revised standard working paper where relevant.
terms.related: Related glossary entries: 002. Service link: Performance Management / Management Reporting; area: Standard costing and variance analysis.
terms.warning: Do not treat the variance as root cause. Use it as a signal, then test price, volume, mix, timing, data and operational explanations before presenting conclusions.
terms.example: Mini-example: if actual cost exceeds the flexed or standard cost, quantify the variance, identify whether price, usage, mix or activity caused it, and assign an owner for follow-up.
terms.alignment: ACCA/CIMA performance management and management accounting practice; standard costing, budgeting and variance-analysis discipline. Not an assurance, audit, tax, legal, investment or valuation conclusion.
terms.title: Direct material Total Variance
